parts.text: Good evening.
My name is Kirsten Lockhart, and I'm running for mayor of the City of Fairfax.
I'd like to thank the League of Women Voters and the Central Fairfax Chamber of Commerce
for hosting this event, and all of you in the audience for being here tonight.
For those of you with whom I haven't had the pleasure to connect with yet, I've been an
appointed member of the City's Planning Commission since March of 2021.
I'm currently the Commission's Vice Chair.
These past five-plus years of service have allowed me to gain deep perspective on the
city, especially on the issues that have been coming up the most this election
cycle. Development, density, what we want the city to look like in 10 or 20 years
from now. I've been fully transparent about my voting record as a planning
commissioner from the start of my campaign. I take pride in doing my
homework, in communicating with stakeholders and residents, in asking the
tough questions, and in being a steward of the city's comprehensive plan. As a
commissioner and now a candidate, I've had the opportunity to engage with and
learn from current and former city staff, elective leadership, boards and
Commission's members and residents themselves. All of them differ in their
visions and priorities but who have all contributed to making Fairfax City the
vibrant 21st century community that our comprehensive plan says we want to be.
Obviously having a front-row seat to city government for the past five and a
half years has deeply influenced my decision to run for office. I believe we
need competent, compassionate leadership from the dais as well as a consistent
data-driven framework for decision-making. Between my commissioner role and my 20
years in strategy and management consulting, I'm confident in my ability to deliver both as your
mayor. But taking a step back from the tactical, running for mayor is also an extension of the
commitment to the city that my family and I made when we moved here in 2017. Like so many of you,
we chose Fairfax City for the services, the schools, the walkability. This is our forever home,
where we are raising our children and where we hopefully will grow old. But whether it's preserving
green space, improving pedestrian and bike safety, or through thoughtful redevelopment that maintains
our good economic health and hopefully enables future young families to make the
same conscious choice to live here, the decisions that we make now must also
serve the next generation. I fully believe we can preserve what makes our
community special while not letting fear of change hold us back. It will take
hard work but it's exactly the kind of hard work that my experience prepared me for.
Well, thank you.
It's great to be with everybody again.
I know I've met many of you as I've served as a council member here in the last two years.

I was a vice president at an investment bank, and I was a division chief for a state wildlife conservation agency.
So I've worked in government, business, academia, and the nonprofit sector.
My specialization in all of that has been working at the community level to build consensus,
to collaborate, and to engage in community problem solving.

Thank you for the opportunity to share what I've heard from residents and neighborhoods across our city.
Two concerns come up repeatedly, redevelopment and rising real estate taxes.
Fairfax City is a 6.4 square mile, largely built out community of about 26,000 people.
Yet too often, our approach to growth seems to assume that the only way to grow is to build up,
with seven, nine, and even 11 story mixed-use projects.
Many residents question whether that is the right path for Fairfax City.
They worry about the added demands on schools, first responders, transportation, water and sewer,
green spaces, increased traffic on roads like Fairfax Boulevard, Main Street, Chainbridge Road,
and Pickett Road. They also worry about the long-term costs of providing services and maintaining
infrastructure. But beyond those concerns, residents are telling me something even more important.
They value Fairfax City's character. We are a city of neighborhoods. Recently, a young couple told
me they chose Fairfax City for their first home because they wanted a community, a neighborhood
of single-family homes, townhouses, or multi-family homes. They work in Roslyn and Arlington, but they
didn't want to live there. They chose Fairfax City because of its small-town character. That
is our competitive advantage. We don't need to become another county jurisdiction. We need to
plan for the future, not the past, and develop a revenue model that doesn't increasingly rely
on ever higher real estate taxes and fees.
